messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Old Memories: Old photos, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi had always known that his childhood was different. Growing up in a traditional Ghanaian household with strict rules and expectations, he learned early on to navigate the complexities of family dynamics. But it wasn't until much later, as an adult looking back, that Kofi began to realize just how far-reaching the effects of those years would be. Kofi's father, a man known for his fiery temper and unyielding discipline, had been a constant source of fear in their home. One particular incident stood out in Kofi's mind - though it was fragmented, like a puzzle with missing pieces. He remembered being around 8 or 9 years old, playing outside when he broke one of the family rules. His father's reaction was swift and merciless: Kofi recalled feeling the sting of his father's belt on his skin, but the specifics were hazy. What lingered instead was the overwhelming sense of helplessness that had washed over him in that moment. Years went by, but Kofi never spoke about what happened. Old photos would occasionally resurface, showing happier times - his parents smiling, family gatherings - and Kofi's mind would instinctively recoil from them. He found it difficult to deliberately recall the memories of those years; trying only made his head spin with anxious thoughts. As he grew older, Kofi learned to avoid situations that felt unpredictable or outside his control. As a principal at a local school, he thrived on routine and order - qualities he had lacked in his own childhood. But even this carefully constructed sense of stability couldn't shield him from the occasional nightmare. Waking up drenched in sweat, with images of chaos still seared into his mind's eye, would leave Kofi shaken for hours. Kofi was terrified that one day, his own anger would boil over and he'd lose control, just like his father before him. This fear simmered beneath the surface of his relationships, including his current partnership. His girlfriend noticed how tightly wound he was at times, but Kofi couldn't quite explain why - even to himself. He felt permanently changed for the worse by what had happened in those childhood years. The memories still lingered with a vividness that normal recollections lacked. When they bubbled up unbidden, as they sometimes did during quiet moments or when old photos resurfaced, Kofi's thoughts would grow muddled and he'd retreat into himself. It was only recently, after an argument with his girlfriend had left him feeling lost and shaken, that Kofi realized just how far these symptoms had carried over into his adult life. He began to recognize patterns of avoidance, the way certain triggers could still transport him back to those days when helplessness seemed absolute. With a dawning sense of trepidation, Kofi sought out therapy, unsure what lay ahead but certain that he couldn't keep living this way - haunted by memories and forever on edge. He wanted to understand why his past continued to hold such sway over him, and how to build a life where those fragmented pieces could finally be set aside.
